claims.text: The modeled material is a single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix with initially minimal dislocation density.
Nanoindentation is performed to 30 Å at 10 m/s and at 300, 600, 900, and 1200 K.
Above 900 K, a sequence of thermally activated microstructural events causes the friction spike and loss of wear resistance.
At 900 K, thermal energy overcomes a stacking-fault-energy barrier.
Overcoming that barrier rapidly annihilates Shockley partial dislocations and collapses stacking faults.
Annihilation of partial dislocations and stacking faults reduces the coating's ability to work-harden.
Near 1200 K, the lattice becomes strongly disordered and approaches localized amorphization within the indentation zone.
The localized disordering or amorphization is promoted by the 10 m/s indentation rate together with thermal softening.
Above 900 K, the stacking fault energy of FeNiCrCoCu decreases and promotes dislocation dissociation.
High strain rate and thermal energy prevent stable dislocation-network formation, producing dislocation starvation.
The 10 m/s loading rate prevents sufficient time for defect recovery, so the response is thermal disordering rather than mechanical annealing.
The Cu matrix facilitates interfacial diffusion near 1200 K because of its lower melting point.
Interfacial diffusion further weakens the coating and contributes to loss of structural integrity.
Loss of crystalline order reduces yield strength and hardness, allowing the indenter to sink with less resistance.
Thermal softening increases the real contact area and thereby raises the friction coefficient.
At 300 and 600 K, stable dislocation activity and work hardening produce high hardness and low friction.
Above 900 K, hardness decreases by more than 50% and the friction coefficient increases by more than a factor of two.
At 1200 K, localized amorphization causes catastrophic wear-resistance loss and may cause material transfer to the indenter.
If mechanical annealing is responsible, reducing the indentation velocity to 1 m/s will produce higher hardness and lower friction than at 10 m/s.
If thermal disordering is responsible, high HCP atom counts and amorphization metrics will persist at 1 m/s together with the friction spike.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts rapid annihilation of Shockley partials and collapse of stacking faults at 900 K, whereas the mechanism says decreasing stacking-fault energy promotes dislocation dissociation. Dissociation ordinarily creates or extends partial-dislocation/stacking-fault configurations, so the opposing changes in stacking-fault population are not reconciled.

The proposed sequence says stacking faults collapse and the region becomes amorphous, but the thermal-disordering criterion expects the HCP atom count to remain high. HCP-classified atoms usually track locally ordered HCP environments or FCC stacking faults, not amorphous atoms, so a high HCP count is not internally consistent as a direct signature of the proposed amorphization.
